content.content:
=== later
later.py: his messages after an entry's creation that may bear on it, though no commit of the
entry followed them (his later word may have gone into a skill or another record instead).

    python3 -I later.py 148                   (or P-148)
    python3 -I later.py 148 --top 25          how many to print (default 15)
    python3 -I later.py 148 --at 36f7db77c --until 2026-10-21T20:54
                                              the entry's text at a commit, and no message after a time

The candidates are his messages in the coordinating sessions (tlib.COORDINATING) from the entry's
creation on (for an entry struck from POSITIONS.md, its last text is read, and the list runs on
past the removal) (the first commit of its trail that made its text), less those that leads.py already
printed near the entry's own commits. Each is scored by the entry's distinctive terms:
  - its title's words, beyond common words (a stop list, and words in more than a tenth of his
    messages), lightly stemmed (possessive and plural off, cut to 7 letters); each weighs its
    rarity in his messages, log(messages / messages holding it);
  - its names in backticks, weight 3 each.
A term in his own words (lines that do not start with ">") counts whole; a term only in the
exchange around his message (the coordinator's message he answered, by the reply chain, its
reply to him, and the lines he quoted) counts half. A message also gains 8 when it falls in the
30 minutes before a commit that changed a file the entry names in backticks (`compiler.md`), other
=== homes
homes.py: where a status that an entry of POSITIONS.md states may already live.

    python3 -I homes.py 151            (or P-151)
    python3 -I homes.py 151 --top 8    candidates per sentence (default 5)
    python3 -I homes.py 151 --at REV   the three files as commit REV holds them

Splits the entry (the working tree's POSITIONS.md; for an entry struck from it, its text as it
last stood, said so at the top) into sentences, and a sentence into its clauses
at the semicolons outside parentheses; a clause keeps the label that opens its sentence, as
"Built:" or "Still to build:". A clause states a status when it, its label or its sentence holds
one of the status words: built, to build, landed, pending, default, waits, standing go, listed for his
review, open, held, parked, owed, taken, stands at, returns after, not moved, and the like.

For each such clause it lists the candidates that may already hold the same point: the numbered
items of review-queue.md's lists (b) and (c), and the lines of PLAN.md (a numbered sub-line also
carries its parent's item number, and its own number as a fork when the parent counts forks).
A candidate is listed when it names the entry or shares a distinctive term with the clause:
  row N, item N (PLAN's), review-queue item N, fork N, way N, batch N, rung X, phase N, ask N,
  decision X, another entry's P-N, a name in backticks (a commit hash too), a dotted finding
  name such as judge-review.1 or A.skeptic.2
=== pointers
pointers.py: every line of the record that names an entry of POSITIONS.md by its number.

    python3 -I pointers.py 86            (or P-86)
    python3 -I pointers.py 86 --at REV   the files as commit REV holds them

Searches, at the working tree: explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, POSITIONS.md, PLAN.md,
review-queue.md, HELD.md and BOOT.md; explorations/reviews/open-asks-*.md; and every file under
.claude/skills/. The history files (POSITIONS-history.md, FACTS-history.md) are not searched:
trail.py reads the first, and both only record. A line counts when it holds the number as a word:
P-86 matches, as in "P-86's" or "(P-86)", but P-860 and P-186 do not. A line that names a range
holding the number ("P-85 to P-88") is listed too, marked as a range.
Prints path:line and the line (cut at 400 characters around the number; --whole prints it whole),
grouped by file; the entry's own line in POSITIONS.md is marked.

=== comments
comments.py: his saved page comments that bear on an entry of POSITIONS.md.

    python3 -I comments.py 66            (or P-66)

He also comments on pages, and those comments are not in the transcripts. They are saved as
explorations/coordinator/positions-audit/evidence/curator-comments-*.md: a section per thread,
headed "## On <what it was anchored to>", with one bullet per comment, "- HH:MM: "words"".
A section counts when its heading, or a comment counts when its own words, either
  - name the entry's number, also as dictated: P-66, P66, PE66, P 66 (not P-660), or
  - quote its title: a quoted run ("..." or curly quotes) of at least three content words, at
    least 60 % of which are words of the entry's bold title (case, possessives and punctuation
    ignored).
A section that counts is printed whole, with its heading; a comment that counts in another
section is printed with that section's heading. Each with its file and line.

=== trail
trail.py: the trail of one entry of POSITIONS.md, from the repository's history.

    python3 -I trail.py 86            (or P-86)
    python3 -I trail.py 86 --short    the commit list only, one line each
    python3 -I trail.py 86 --at REV   the record as commit REV holds it

Prints:
  1. the entry's text at HEAD (for an entry struck from POSITIONS.md: STRUCK at the top, with the
     commit that removed it and the reason its history block gives, and the text as it last stood);
  2. its blocks in POSITIONS-history.md at HEAD, each with the commit that wrote it (the oldest
     commit whose history file holds the block's provenance line). A block's own "commit X" names
     the source it cites, not its writer;
  3. every commit that made or changed the entry's text, oldest first, read from each commit's own
     tree (side branches included): hash, UTC author time, subject, what it did, how the link to
     the text before was made (number, line, title: exact; similarity: score printed), how many
     other entries of POSITIONS.md the commit changed, and the reasons on record: the history
     blocks it wrote, the comments above verbatim copies of the text in the old history file, and
     the commit message.
  4. a cross-check: the old history lines that the numbering block names as earlier texts of this
     entry, and whether each is a text of this trail.
=== quote
quote.py: does the curator's message at a UTC time hold a quote word for word?

    python3 -I quote.py "QUOTE" 2026-09-26T10:21:32Z
    python3 -I quote.py "QUOTE" 2026-09-26T10:21        a prefix: every message of his in that minute

The time is a prefix of his message's timestamp, as show.py takes it (a trailing Z is dropped).
For each message of his at that time it prints one verdict:
  EXACT        the quote is a substring of the message as stored
  NORMALISED   a substring once both have every run of whitespace made one space, ends trimmed,
               and the curly apostrophe U+2019 made a straight one (nothing else is changed)
  NO MATCH     neither; it then prints the longest run of the quote's words that the
               message holds word for word (after the same normalising), for a reader to judge
With the match it prints the message's text around it.

=== near
near.py: the curator's messages in a window before a UTC time, each with the coordinating
session's message that it answered, found along the transcript's reply chain.

- **2b. Narrow the sentence to the rule.** A `where`-clause variable may stand in an `extends` clause when the declaration's constraints fix it to one type for each instance. A callout says that neither path runs it yet, and a ledger row holds the gap until a checker and walk rung builds it.

**How they weigh.**

- 2a matches both paths and the later calculi, and costs one sentence. It gives up a convenience: a fixed variable is inferred from `S` instead of written as a parameter. No code on record uses that.
- 2b matches the rule exactly and keeps more of the Working Draft. It gives up agreement between the text and both paths: the text then promises a form that neither path runs, a gap the specification's revision is meant to close, and a later rung must build it.

**Recommendation.** 2a, keep the sentence and record its breadth as chosen. Default: 2a.

References:

1. The question's home: PLAN, "Pavol's answers, in the order they are needed", item 14; review-queue item 41.
2. The sentence and the examples: `Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:368-380` (the sentence and its callout), `:382-395` (the covariance idiom), `:428-466` (the trait over every instantiation), `:469-513` (`Empty` and the library's shape); the calculus, `Specification/appendices/calculi/where/`.
3. The fixed case, and the breadth no one decided: `explorations/reviews/batch-5-conformance.md:115-120`, `:142-153`, `:256`.
4. The later word: P-25 and P-26; `Papers/Welterweight/fig-grammar.tick:4-18`, `Papers/Welterweight/grammar.tick:42-47`; `research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019-extract.md`.
5. The library: the widening function, `Library/CovariantCollection.fss:15-35`, and ledger row 17; `Nothing[\T\]`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1007`; the comments, `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1005-1006` (Maessen, 2008, as `batch-5-conformance.md:132` dates it) and `Library/TypeProxy.fsi:33-35`.
6. The paths: F-21; F-167; ledger rows 17 and 331.
7. The model: `explorations/reviews/batch-5-conformance.md:120`.
8. The bare `Nothing`: P-90.

### Ask 3. The bound on the element type of `Vector` and `Matrix`

**The question.** Do `Vector` and `Matrix` keep the bound `T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }` on their element type, as landed?

**The context.**

------
**P4. The `where` clauses, 13 sites.** The sites are the fused reduction pairs, 6 (row 433: `SumReduction`'s two `distribute` overloads and `MaxSumReductionPair` and `MinSumReductionPair` name `MaxReduction[\T\]` and `MinReduction[\T\]`, whose bounds `T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]` does not meet; the row's fix is `where { T extends StandardMax[\T\] }` on each method, or dropping both pairs); `AnyList`'s operations, 4 (row 636, under the team's comment `Not yet: comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]`, `Library/List.fsi:56`); the identities' numeral fallback, 2 (row 436, its designed fix the specification's `HasIdentity`); and the list half of the comparisons, 1 (row 634, `LexicographicOrder`'s `CMP` at `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2063`; the judgement's way is `List[\E\] extends LexicographicOrder[\List[\E\],E\] where { E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\] }`, with a structural `=` kept on `List`). The ask needs, for each site, whether a library line clears it without a `where` clause, as `Nothing[\T\]` did for `Maybe`, and what each form of `where` clause costs on the checker, walk, the code generator and the specification. The coordinator's drafted brief (`batch16/brief-probe-where.md`, in its scratchpad) covers rows 433, 636 and 436, with row 677 beside them (the checker takes a `where` clause's new names and drops its constraints) and row 701 in one paragraph (the code generator's refusal). It should add: the list half; the type variable in a listed type of a `comprises` clause, which the revival's widened proviso admits (review-queue item 42, default the widened text) and which row 636's repair needs, with a count of the team's commented clauses of that shape (`Integral`'s, F-121; `List`'s; by a search for this draft, eight in `Library/Reflect.fss`, one on `HasRank`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:1908-1909`, and one on `SkipList`'s `Node`, `Library/SkipList.fss:100-107`); whether the type group's later form, bounds on declared static parameters only, with lower as well as upper bounds on a method's own parameters (`Papers/Welterweight/fig-grammar.tick:17-18`, `grammar.tick:42-47`), can state row 433's condition on a method without a `where` clause; and what ask 1's answer requires of the build. Its report: `explorations/perf-probes/where-clauses/REPORT.md`. Then the ask: build the specification's `where` clauses before the switch-over, and which forms (a condition on a method, conditional extension, a type variable in a listed type), or clear the 13 sites by the library's own lines; with the proviso of item 42 folded in.

**P5. The array sites, 21.** The sites are 14 bodies of `Vector` and `Matrix` typed by their parent trait (`ivmap`, `map`, `fill` and `tabulate` are declared on `Array1` and `Array2`, so `Vector`'s `+` answers an `Array1` where it declares a `Vector`; `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2526` to `:2977`); 3 bodies that test a size in a `typecase`, `typecase N[\b0\] of N[\0\] => r`, where the checker does not learn in the arm that `b0` is 0 (`:2551`, `:2562`, `:2946`; P-55 makes the arm reachable); 2 export errors (`:12`: one names the api's dead sizes and its 2D and 3D factories, the other a list of traits across the library); and `Col` and `Row` called on an unsized `Array` (`:2697`, `:2701`, row 678). No worker has written their ways. The coordinator's drafted brief (`batch16/brief-probe-arrays.md`) covers them: the library's own ways first (an override in the narrower trait, the `cast` device, a `typecase` on a size), the ways that would touch P-40, P-85 or P-87 named rather than taken, shadow patches measured with walk's array tests, microGPT's quick walk check where a patched declaration is one microGPT calls, and one distance run. It should run after ask 3, since the 14 bodies sit under that bound, and say which entries of the export error are the dead sizes, which go only with the switch-over's design (P-40). Its report: `explorations/perf-probes/array-sites/REPORT.md`.

## 4. Settled already

- **`embiggen`'s site (row 631, 1 site): not an ask.** P-27 sets the way: the library's own typed shape, `MapReduceReduction[\R\](j, z: R)` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:3691`), which `MIMapReduceReduction` and `embiggen` would follow (`:3700`, `:3714`). The review queue sorts it as routine (item 124). Its cost is on record: the declared types of its callers in `Library/Map.fss:197`, `Library/IntMap.fss`, `Library/PrefixMap.fss`, `Library/Pairs.fss:75` and the team test `ProjectFortress/tests/WordCountSmall.fss:76` (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-generator-slips/REPORT.md:160`). So it is the coordinator's call for the next library rung, listed for his review. It comes back as an ask only if that rung finds that a walk value moves, or if the coordinator reads his word on the team's demos as covering the team test.
- **The list half's other way, a bound on the list's element.** P-42 rules it out: the library instantiates its generic containers at tuples, and a bound on `LexicographicOrder`'s element would make a list of tuples, functions or `()` impossible to write (`explorations/reviews/tuple-comparisons-judgement.md`, way 1c). So the list half waits on the `where` clauses (P4).
- **The bare `Nothing` (row 331; F-21).** P-90: not tried before `where` clauses work. A point for the coordinator, not an ask: the specification's own "Not allowed" `Empty` shows that a singleton extending `List[\T\]` for every `T` is refused by instantiation exclusion with or without a `where` clause (`Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:469-513`), and F-167's sentence bars its form. So building `where` clauses will not reopen it, and P-90's wording, which ties it to them, may want a line.
- **Arithmetic in a size, the first array fork.** P-55, answered.
- **The element width, the model's sized types, and the store that puts `double[]` under the generic traits, the last three array forks.** P-85: open with no default, and returning after the switch-over. The model's sized types are also P-87's: a diff shown to him before anything is built, in phase 5. When they return, the order is the width, then the model's types, then the store, since every type line of the model's diff and every store follows from the width (`explorations/reviews/array-design-ways.md`, section 8). Owed before then: their plain explainers (review-queue item 37), and an answer to his question why `RR64` and not `RR32`; the one reason on record is the Python reference's float64 values (P-85).
- **The api's dead sizes, one of the two export sites.** P-40: they go only by a diff shown to him with the switch-over's design (PLAN item 12; `explorations/reviews/decision-d-diff/rebase-2026-09-29/library-e3.patch`, which applies).
- **Arithmetic on `Number`, as a way for ask 3.** P-43, route A: not offered.

**The fusion.** Kento Emoto of the University of Tokyo wrote it in 2010, in a research collaboration with Sun. His library makes "generators of generators": all the prefixes, suffixes or runs of a list. You write a problem the obvious slow way, and the library rewrites it into one fast pass, using an algebraic law.
- **Example:** the largest sum of any run of adjacent numbers in [3, −5, 4, −1, 2]. The slow way sums each of the 15 runs and takes the best: 4 + (−1) + 2 = 5. The fused way gets the same answer in one pass over the list.
- **The law:** adding spreads over taking a maximum, a + max(b, c) = max(a+b, a+c).
- **Is it kernel fusion?** You're close. Like kernel fusion, nested loops become one. Unlike it, the algorithm itself changes, and an algebraic law justifies the change. It's the same style as Steele's talks.

**The fusion.** Kento Emoto of the University of Tokyo wrote it in 2010, in a research collaboration with Sun. His library makes "generators of generators": all the prefixes, suffixes or runs of a list. You write a problem the obvious slow way, and the library rewrites it into one fast pass, using an algebraic law.
- **Example:** the largest sum of any run of adjacent numbers in [3, −5, 4, −1, 2]. The slow way sums each of the 15 runs and takes the best: 4 + (−1) + 2 = 5. The fused way gets the same answer in one pass over the list.
- **The law:** adding spreads over taking a maximum, a + max(b, c) = max(a+b, a+c).
- **Is it kernel fusion?** You're close. Like kernel fusion, nested loops become one. Unlike it, the algorithm itself changes, and an algebraic law justifies the change. It's the same style as Steele's talks.

Since then the checker has learned to allow overloads that differ in their type parameters, so their fix may work now. Nobody has measured it.

**Removal.** I agree it's a poor default. It deletes a working idea of the team's, and the answers stay the same only because the slow way computes them too.

**The run-time `cast`.** `cast[\T\](x)` is the library's own checked conversion, like Swift's `as!`. When the program runs, it checks that `x` is a `T` and returns it as one, or throws `CastError`. The checker then trusts it. The trade is that the checker proves less and the run time checks instead.

**The compiled side.** Every `where` form the library keeps must also be compiled after the switch-over, and the code generator refuses all of them today.
- Method conditions are cheap: one check removed.
- Conditional extension is real work: the class loader must make a list class comparable only where its elements are.

The function \EXP{\mathrm{coerce}} returns its argument as the given type.


\section{Convenience Types}
\seclabel{convenience-types}

An optional value \VAR{v} of type \EXP{\TYP{Maybe}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}
is either \EXP{\TYP{Nothing}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket} or
\EXP{\TYP{Just}(v)} declared as follows:
%(* Optional Values *)
%trait Maybe[\T\] comprises { Nothing[\T\], Just[\T\] }
%  isNothing: Boolean
%end
%value object Nothing[\T\] extends Maybe[\T\]
%end
%object Just[\T\](just: T) extends Maybe[\T\]
%end
\begin{Fortress}
\(\mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  Optional Values \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
\(\KWD{trait}\:\TYP{Maybe}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket \KWD{comprises} \{\,\TYP{Nothing}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket, \TYP{Just}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket\,\}\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \VAR{isNothing}\COLON \TYP{Boolean}\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{value}\;\;\KWD{object}\:\TYP{Nothing}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket \KWD{extends}\:\TYP{Maybe}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket\)\\
\(\KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{object}\:\TYP{Just}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(\VAR{just}\COLON T) \KWD{extends}\:\TYP{Maybe}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket\)\\
\(\KWD{end}\)
\end{Fortress}
The empty case is one object for each type \VAR{T},
and each use writes the type,
as in \EXP{\TYP{Nothing}\llbracket\TYP{String}\rrbracket}.
The following declaration of a single \TYP{Nothing} for every
instantiation of \TYP{Maybe} is not allowed:
%(* Not allowed! *)
%object Nothing extends Maybe[\T\] excludes Just[\T\] where {T extends Object}
%end
\begin{Fortress}
\(\mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  Not allowed! \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
\(\KWD{object} \TYP{Nothing} \KWD{extends} \TYP{Maybe}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket \KWD{excludes} \TYP{Just}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket \KWD{where} \{T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Object}\}\)\\
\(\KWD{end}\)
\end{Fortress}
It would make \TYP{Nothing} a \EXP{\TYP{Maybe}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}
for every \VAR{T} at once,
which instantiation exclusion forbids (\secref{where-clauses});
and an object declaration has no \KWD{excludes} clause
(\secref{object-decls}), an object trait type already excluding
every type that is not its supertype (\secref{object-traits}).
\revision{revival-nothing}{The Working Draft of February 2011 declared
\TYP{Nothing} with the declaration marked ``Not allowed''.
The declaration of \EXP{\TYP{Nothing}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket} is the
library's, whose own source says it
``will become a non-parametric singleton when we get where clauses working'';
instantiation exclusion closes that road.}
======

\subsection{The empty optional value}
\seclabel{revival-nothing}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \secref{convenience-types};
\secref{chained-exceptions}; \chapref{lib:exception}.
\item[Change] \TYP{Nothing} becomes
\EXP{\KWD{value}\;\;\KWD{object}\:\TYP{Nothing}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}
extending \EXP{\TYP{Maybe}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}, with no
\KWD{excludes} clause, and \TYP{Maybe} comprises
\EXP{\TYP{Nothing}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket} and
\EXP{\TYP{Just}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}; the original declaration is kept,
marked ``Not allowed''. The defaults of an exception's message and chain
become \EXP{\TYP{Nothing}\llbracket\TYP{String}\rrbracket} and
\EXP{\TYP{Nothing}\llbracket\TYP{Exception}\rrbracket}.
\item[Rationale] The original makes \TYP{Nothing} a
\EXP{\TYP{Maybe}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket} for every \VAR{T} at once. Its
\KWD{excludes} clause is also one the grammar gives no object declaration
(\secref{object-decls}), and is redundant, an object trait type already
excluding every type that is not its supertype (\secref{object-traits}).
The replacement is the library's declaration.
\item[Effect] The empty case is written with its type, as in
\EXP{\TYP{Nothing}\llbracket\TYP{String}\rrbracket}, until the static
arguments of a generic object can be inferred from the type expected.
The compiled path's own library, used until the one library replaces it,
still declares a single \TYP{Nothing} with a coercion to every

\EXP{\TYP{Nothing}\llbracket\TYP{String}\rrbracket}
(row~331 of the revival's gap ledger).

content.content:
## 5. The decision

**The specification's spelling of the empty case was taken, not the corpus's**: `Maybe[\T\] comprises { Just[\T\], NothingObject[\T\] }` with `coerce(_: Nothing) = NothingObject[\T\]` and a separate `value object Nothing end`. This was a decision, and the code did not force it.

**The two candidates cannot coexist, measured.** `probes/DualNothing.fss` declares both spellings of one name in one scope under local names — `value object NothingD[\T extends Any\] extends MaybeD[\T\]` and then `value object NothingD end`. `probes/DualNothing.txt`: the non-parametric declaration takes the name, and both the parametric declaration's own header (`:16`) and the `comprises` clause that mentions it (`:8`) become errors — "Incorrect number of static arguments for type 'NothingD': provided 1, expected 0". So the fork is binary and there is no overload that serves both spellings.

**Why the specification cannot simply be transcribed.** `probes/WhereClauseNothing.fss` is `convenience.tex:49` under local names — `object NothingW extends MaybeW[\T\] where {T extends Object}`. `probes/WhereClauseNothing.txt` records the same single error from `fortress compile` and from `fortress walk`, both rc=255: `T is undefined`, at the `T` inside the extends clause. Name resolution does not let a where clause bind a type variable used in an extends clause, on either path, so neither implementation can express the declaration the specification writes; `CodeGen.java:4088` (`forObjectDeclPrePass`, `header.getWhereClause().isNone()`) would refuse it at codegen even if name resolution admitted it. The compensating mechanism is coercion, which the compile path has and the interpreter does not (`explorations/coordinator/map/spec-to-implementation.md:288`: "nothing: no occurrence of `Coercion` or `coerce` anywhere under `interpreter/`"). That is why the team's draft for this world spells the empty case as it does and the interpreter's prelude does not: the interpreter had no way to write it, and said so at `FortressLibrary.fss:1340-1341`.

**What decided it.** Three things point one way. The prose says `Nothing` is one object (`convenience.tex:49`) and uses it as a value at a `Maybe[\String\]` (`exceptions.tex:122`). The team, writing for *this* world, chose that shape (`CompilerLibrary.fsi:217-229`) and used it in all seven of its own draft tests. And the interpreter's own author records that the parametric form is a workaround for a missing feature, not the design. The compiler world has the compensating feature, and `probes/MaybeCoercionSites.txt` records it working in all three positions the specification writes an unparameterised `Nothing` in — a declared-type binding, a getter's default, a function argument — with `typecase` confirming the coerced value is a `NothingObject[\ZZ32\]` at run time. Against that stands corpus usage, which is evidence of what was written, not of what the language is (rule 4).

**The alternative and its cost.** Taking the corpus's `Nothing[\T\]` would remove the one error each of `ExceptionScoping.fss` and `oddJuxt.fss` now carries — neither names anything else the compile path lacks, though neither was measured reaching a run, so "clear" means clear of errors and not shown to pass — and would spare the later library route the renames in `List.fss`, `Set.fss`, `Map.fss` and `PureList.fss`. Its cost is that `= Nothing`, the only spelling of a `Maybe` value the prose chapters ever write, would be a static error in the compiler world for good, and this world would carry the interpreter's acknowledged workaround for a feature it does not need the workaround for. The library route is a reserved fork and those files will be rewritten line by line when it opens; `convenience.tex` will not be rewritten. Two ladder files whose spelling the specification does not sanction were judged the smaller loss, and they are not lost silently: they become ledger row 331 in `record.md`, which names the spelling, both probes, and where the fix lies.

**A second decision: beside `Option`, not over it.** `Maybe` is a second copy of the `Condition` protocol rather than built on `Option`. Three ways to build it over `Option` were considered and rejected. Making `Maybe[\T\]` extend `Option[\T\]` fails because `Option` is declared `comprises { NoneObject[\E19\], Some[\E19\] }` (`CompilerBuiltin.fsi:650`) and a `comprises` clause is closed, so it would have to be widened — a change to a declared type the prelude already has, which `CLIMB-BATCH-1.md` reserves as a stop. Making `Just`/`NothingObject` wrap a `Some`/`NoneObject` field would put an indirection and an allocation under every method to save one-line bodies. A type alias is not available: `Specification/fortress/preamble.tex:81` lists type aliases among the features not yet supported. The copy costs 56 lines of one-line bodies in `CompilerLibrary.fss`; that was judged cheaper than any of the three, and it is also what the team's draft does — its `Maybe` extends `Condition[\T\]`, not `Option`.

**A third, smaller: the commented draft was replaced, not left beside the live code.** `CompilerLibrary.fsi:217-229` now holds live declarations in place of the comment. Leaving the comment beside working declarations of the same names would be a stale second answer in the source, and `explorations/protocol.md` keeps rationale out of the tree. The draft is quoted in full in §4 of this report and recoverable at `git show cb242a2d8:Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`, so nothing is lost.

type, not from a field's declared type. In every position probed, a reference
to a generic object written without its static arguments is a **static error**
on the compiled path and an `InterpreterBug` under `walk`; writing the static
argument out makes the identical program compile, run and print on both paths.

A \KWD{where} clause may include mutually recursive constraints.
All static variables in a trait, object, or functional declaration must
occur either as a static parameter or as a \KWD{where}-clause variable.
\appref{where-calculus} describes a Fortress core calculus with
\KWD{where} clauses.

An entry of an \KWD{extends} clause may carry a \KWD{where} clause of its
own (\secref{trait-decls}).
If that clause introduces no \KWD{where}-clause variable and all its
constraints are trait constraints, the declared trait or object extends the
entry's type exactly where the constraints hold:
an instance whose static arguments satisfy them is of that type,
and an instance whose static arguments do not satisfy them is not.
The constraints hold while the entry itself, the declaration's value
parameters and its members are checked, as if they were in the
declaration's own \KWD{where} clause.
The rest of the declaration holds at every instance and is checked
without them: its static parameters, its own \KWD{where} clause, its
\KWD{throws} clause and contract, its \KWD{excludes} and \KWD{comprises}
clauses, and the other entries of its \KWD{extends} clause.
So a list is totally ordered exactly where its elements are:

A \KWD{where}-clause variable may not appear as a static argument
in an \KWD{extends} clause.
Such an occurrence would make the declared trait or object a subtype of
one instantiation for each type that the variable may stand for,
which instantiation exclusion forbids
(\secref{trait-types} and \secref{trait-decls});
the second of the three declarations below shows why.
\revision{revival-where}{This restriction is new.
The three declarations that follow were offered as legal by the
Working Draft of February 2011; they are kept as examples of what is not
allowed, each with the way to write it.}

In particular, a trait declaration may not extend other instantiations
of itself through a \KWD{where}-clause variable.
The following declaration would express that the static parameter \VAR{S}
of \VAR{C} is covariant, making \EXP{C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket} a subtype of
\EXP{C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket} for every supertype \VAR{T} of \VAR{S};
it is not allowed:
%(* Not allowed! *)
%trait C[\S\] extends C[\T\]
%  where {S extends T, T extends Object}
%end
\begin{Fortress}
\(\mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  Not allowed! \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
\(\KWD{trait} C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket \KWD{extends} C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{where} \{S \KWD{extends} T, T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Object}\}\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)
\end{Fortress}
